prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping, which brought atomic timekeeping to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: Having read all eight opening ballots, I move my preferred configuration from my own first choice, B014, to B015. Optical lattice clocks are the one candidate that most of the committee ranks highly for independent reasons: Kroll and Lindroth place it first, Olsson second, and every member ranks it somewhere in their eight. As an experimentalist I value what it offers: a clear originating idea (Katori's magic-wavelength trapping, which removes the light shift while keeping Lamb-Dicke confinement of many atoms), a compact attribution to two people (Katori for the concept and first strontium clock, Ye for taking performance to the systematic-uncertainty frontier), and a result already reproduced in laboratories on several continents (JILA, RIKEN, PTB, SYRTE, NIST) with agreement near 10^-18 and clock comparisons that stand as independent confirmation. It is an instrument-driven advance that also opens fundamental physics, namely tests of constant variation and relativistic redshift at millimetre scales. Compared with B014, where credit in a collaboration of hundreds is the central difficulty, the attribution here is the cleanest on the shortlist. Compared with B018 and B003, no early theorist or experimental pioneer is stranded by the three-name limit.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is novelty and timing. Precision laser spectroscopy and frequency combs were recognised in 2005 (Hall, Hansch) and the control of single ions in 2012 (Wineland, Haroche), so some members will see lattice clocks as the next step in a line already honoured, and a prize might be better spent on a field not yet recognised. The redefinition of the SI second has not happened, so a sceptic can say the decisive application milestone still lies ahead. Other clock groups (Lemonde, Ludlow, Lisdat, and the ion-clock work of Rosenband and Wineland's group) have credible claims that two names cannot represent. Finally, I am dropping my own first choice, and I should be honest that B014 is a stronger candidate on the dimension of opening a wholly new observational window.

responses.point: Ranks lattice clocks first: original, conceptually clean, the logical continuation of the Nobel line from precision spectroscopy to combs, and arguably overdue; also declares a research stay at the Hall laboratory where Ye is associated.
responses.response: I agree with the scientific case and I give weight to your point that independent laboratories confirm the 10^-18 performance. I would qualify two things. First, 'overdue' should not be taken as a reason for ranking: a prize's urgency is a separate matter from the discovery's merit. Second, your Hall-laboratory connection is declared as background, which is appropriate, but since Ye is one of the two proposed names I think the committee should record it formally and weigh your support for B015 accordingly. My own case rests on the attribution and on the independent confirmation, which do not rely on your testimony about the laboratory.

responses.point: Ranks B015 sixth because Ye's frequency-comb work is arguably partly within the 2005 prize, and overlap with Hall-Hansch and Wineland may reduce novelty; also notes that Lemonde, Gill and the NIST groups contributed to demonstrations.
responses.response: This is the most serious objection and I only partly accept it. The 2005 prize recognised the comb as a tool for measuring optical frequencies; the lattice clock is a different invention, since the magic wavelength resolves the conflict between long interrogation of many atoms and light shifts, and no earlier prize citation describes it. The 2012 prize concerned manipulation of single quantum systems, whereas a lattice clock gets its stability from averaging over thousands of atoms. I agree, however, that the citation must be worded around the lattice concept and its performance so that it does not read as a return to combs, and I accept your caution that other groups' contributions to the first demonstrations are real and not fully allocated by the supplied names.

responses.point: Ranks IceCube first as a clear, nameable discovery of nature that ties particle physics to astrophysics, with a compact Halzen-Karle pair, while flagging that the 2002 neutrino-astronomy prize requires careful framing of novelty and that two names may not fairly represent a large collaboration.
responses.response: I ranked B014 first myself, and I still think it is the discovery with the greatest reach. I do not dispute your scientific case. My disagreement is about the prize configuration: your own uncertainty about whether two names fairly represent a collaboration of hundreds, together with Eriksson's note that Kowalski, Klein and Waxman and the AMANDA and DUMAND pioneers are outside the credit, persuades me that B014 is the less safe prize this year. Source identification beyond TXS 0506+056 and NGC 1068 is also statistically modest. I would keep B014 as my first alternative and revisit it in later rounds, since I do not think the committee should dismiss it.

responses.point: Ranks lattice clocks first: Katori's magic-wavelength concept and Ye-group realisations give a clear, original invention with agreement at 1e-18 across laboratories and a stable interpretation, and she regards the two-person credit as fair.
responses.response: I agree and would add a reason from the experimental side that supports your point on independent confirmation: the agreement is not only between similar devices but across species (Sr, Yb) and across institutions through optical-fibre and satellite comparisons, which tests the systematic uncertainty budgets rather than repeating one design. Since you note that this is a field you know from the theory side, I would ask the committee to treat the experimental question of whether Ye's 10^-18 systematic budgets are truly independent of Katori's by examining the comparison data directly, and not take the agreement on trust.

responses.point: Ranks fluctuation theorems first as the strongest fundamental-theory candidate, and ranks B015 fourth as a clean, uncontested two-name allocation, noting that the question is whether the committee wants to wait for the SI second redefinition.
responses.response: Your statement that the B015 allocation is clean and uncontested matters to me, because it is the point on which B015 beats B014, B018 and B003. On waiting for the redefinition of the second, I would not wait: the Nobel criteria concern discovery and invention, and the redefinition is a metrological decision of a different body that follows the science. As for B005, with only one member ranking it, I do not see a basis yet to support it, but your argument that the Jarzynski and Crooks relations are exact and widely tested is a serious one, and I would be glad to hear what experimental confirmation you regard as decisive beyond single-molecule pulling.

responses.point: Ranks circuit QED first, with a theory proposal (Blais) and first strong-coupling experiments (Wallraff, Schoelkopf), but acknowledges the 2025 circuit-based prize and that Girvin and Huang are outside the credited names.
responses.response: I find the circuit QED case strong but I place it below B015 for the reasons you give yourself: the founding credit extends beyond the three supplied names, and the 2025 recognition of macroscopic quantum effects in superconducting circuits makes a return to the same technology this soon harder to justify. I would not call it a reason to reject B039, and I would be willing to rank it above B032 if the committee wants a quantum-information choice, but I do not think it should displace a candidate whose attribution is cleaner.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the lattice clock as distinct from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 prize on single quantum systems, or sees it as a continuation of the same line.
Whether the first demonstrations of lattice clocks and the 10^-18 performance can be fairly assigned to two names when Lemonde, Ludlow, Lisdat and other groups contributed.

Whether to treat B014 as the better prize if the committee is prepared to accept a two-name credit for a very large collaboration; I have not resolved how to weigh the opening of neutrino astronomy against its attribution difficulty.
My recollection of the history and of the latest uncertainty values is from general knowledge and has not been verified here.
statement.conflict_note: I have no recorded personal or institutional connection to Hidetoshi Katori or Jun Ye, and none is apparent from my profile for B015. For the alternative B014 my work in astroparticle physics (PAMELA, Fermi-LAT, balloon polarimetry) is in a neighbouring field but I have no documented tie to IceCube or its named candidates, so I see no recusal issue; I note this field closeness as a possible bias in my earlier first-place ranking. I note that Kroll declares a research stay at a laboratory associated with Ye.
